questions.q: What is the four-step pattern this lesson teaches for responding to a technical objection?
options: Acknowledge, clarify, answer, check
Deny, defend, dismiss, move on
Answer, acknowledge, apologize, concede
Clarify, debate, escalate, check
questions.explain: Acknowledge the concern, clarify any ambiguity before guessing, answer the specific concern raised, then check that the answer actually landed -- skipping clarify is the most common mistake.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say answering with a prepared response that's 'adjacent to' the real objection, rather than the objection actually asked, is costly?
options: Because prepared answers are always factually wrong
Because boards notice quickly, and an answer that doesn't address the specific concern reads as not having understood it or deliberately dodging it -- both worse than a shorter, exact answer
Because review boards forbid the use of any prepared material
Because it has no real effect on how the response is received
questions.explain: An answer that doesn't actually address the raised concern reads as either misunderstanding or dodging -- both read worse to a board than a shorter answer that correctly addresses what was actually asked.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the best way to correct a reviewer whose objection is based on a misreading of your design?
options: Ignore the objection since it's based on a misunderstanding
Visibly show frustration that the reviewer didn't understand the design correctly
Precisely restate what the design actually does, without a tone implying the reviewer wasn't paying attention
Agree with the incorrect objection to avoid conflict
questions.explain: Correcting the record precisely, without a rebuke-toned correction, fixes the misunderstanding cleanly. Getting visibly frustrated -- even when factually right -- reads worse to a board than the original misunderstanding.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what distinguishes a scope-creep objection from a genuine design flaw, and why does the distinction matter?
options: There is no real distinction -- all objections should be treated identically

A scope-creep objection pushes the design to handle something outside the stated requirements; treating every out-of-scope question as a flaw wastes limited time, while wrongly dismissing a real in-scope gap as 'out of scope' also costs credibility
Scope-creep objections should always be dismissed outright with no further comment
Genuine design flaws should always be reframed as out of scope to avoid admitting them
questions.explain: A scope-creep objection pushes beyond the stated requirements; a genuine flaw is a real in-scope gap. Getting the distinction wrong in either direction costs credibility -- over-investing in out-of-scope hypotheticals, or wrongly waving away a real gap as out of scope.

questions.q: Per this lesson's discussion of Salesforce's CTA review board, why is 'defend and revise' described as a meaningfully different skill from pure defense?
options: Because candidates are never allowed to change their original solution under any circumstances
Because it means treating a sharp, well-founded objection as new information that might genuinely change the answer, rather than deflecting it purely to avoid looking like you changed your mind
Because CTA judges only evaluate whether a candidate holds their original position no matter what
Because revising a solution is always a sign of a weak original design
questions.explain: Training material on the CTA board describes judges expecting candidates to genuinely revise a solution when an objection exposes something it should handle differently -- holding an indefensible position just to avoid appearing to change your mind is the weaker move, not the stronger one.
